[EXECUTIVE SUMMARY]

This is the Annual National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for the FY 2019/20 which has been prepared in line with Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which require the Controller of Budget to submit to Parliament quarterly budget implementation reports for the National and County Governments every four months. The report presents cumulatively budget performance for FY 2019/20.

During the financial year, receipts into the consolidated fund amounted to Kshs.2.58 trillion , representing 97.8 per cent of the revised annual target of Kshs.2.65 trillion, a slight decline compared to Kshs.2.60 trillion received in the FY 2018/19. Total exchequer issues to MDAs, Consolidated Funds Service (CFS) and County Governments amounted to Kshs.2.53 trillion representing 92.5 per cent of the revised net estimates, a decline compared to 95.6 per cent recorded in the FY 2018/19. This comprised of Kshs.1.8 trillion for recurrent expenditure, Kshs.385.8 billion for development expenditure and Kshs.316 billion to the County Governments. Exchequer issues to counties comprised of Kshs.286.8 billion and Kshs.29.2 billion as equatable share and conditional grants respectively.

These included; approval of Supplementary Budgets too close to the end of the financial year, therefore not allowing time for budget implementation and non-alignment of Supplementary Budgets to actual performance by MDAs resulting to a reduction below the level of expenditure already incurred. The office of the Controller of Budget recommends that Supplementary Budgets should not be approved too close to year-end. The National Treasury should liaise with MDAs when effecting budget revisions to align reallocations to budget performance. Further, Accounting Officers should ensure timely submission of financial reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget in line with Section 83 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012 to allow for timely preparation and publication of Budget Implementation Review Reports. Ministries, Departments and Agencies with pending bills should ensure their payments are prioritized as the first charge in the FY 2020/21 before embarking on new development projects. Finally, the office of the Auditor-General should conduct a special audit of the funds released towards COVID-19 pandemic interventions to give an assurance on value for money and whether the funds were utilized as required by the law.

[1  INTRODUCTION]

Article 228 of the Constitution of Kenya established the Office of the Controller of Budget with the mandate to oversee the implementation of the budgets of the National and County Governments by authorizing withdrawals from public funds under Articles 204, 206 and 207 of the Constitution and to report on the implementation of the budgets to each House of Parliament every four months. This report fulfils the requirement of Article 228(6), of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016 by presenting information on the budget implementation by National Government MDAs in the FY 2019/20.

The report outlines budget performance by MDAs in FY 2019/20. It is organised into seven chapters. Chapter one offers an introduction. Chapter two provides a summary of receipts into the Consolidated Fund in the FY 2019/20. It also provides a breakdown on the disbursement of funds received into the Consolidated Fund to fund expenditure for MDAs, Consolidated Fund Services and to the fortyseven counties for both development and recurrent programmes.

Chapter three presents the overall budget performance. It presents summary performance for both development and recurrent expenditure by the MDAs and funds transferred to County Governments as shareable revenue and from Development Partners. It also presents Consolidated Fund Services performance which is discussed under recurrent expenditure. Consolidated Fund Services provides information on Public debt; Pensions and Gratuities; and Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional Officeholders and Miscellaneous Services. The chapter also presents expenditure by economic classifications by the MDAs, for development and recurrent votes and identifies current and capital transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies.

[3.3.1 Public Debt]

The revised allocation towards repayment of public debt in FY 2019/20 amounted to Kshs.778.85 billion representing a decline of 8.2 per cent from Kshs.848.3 billion allocated in the FY 2018/19. This allocation comprised of Kshs.532.5 billion and Kshs.253.35 billion for internal and external debt respectively. The internal debt comprised of Kshs.301.81 billion for interest payment and Kshs.223.68 billion for redemptions. On the other hand, external debt comprised of Kshs.131.87 billion towards payment of interest and Kshs.121.48 billion for redemption.

During the reporting period, actual expenditure on public debt was Kshs.717.65 billion. This amount represented 92.1 per cent of the revised gross estimates, which was a decline compared to 96.8 per cent (Kshs.821.3 billion) recorded in FY 2018/19. The decline is explained by the repayment of a commercial loan of USD.1 billion (Kshs.101,529 million) syndicated loan and USD.750 million (Kshs.77,722 million) debut international sovereign bond which matured in FY 2018/19.

As at 30th June 2020, the gross public debt stood at Kshs.6.69 trillion recording a 15.3 per cent growth compared to Kshs.5.80 trillion as at 30th June 2019. External debt grew by Kshs.492.67 billion while Domestic debt grew by Kshs.393.1 billion. [3.3.1 Public Debt]

As at 30th June 2020, the gross public debt stood at Kshs.6.69 trillion recording a 15.3 per cent growth compared to Kshs.5.80 trillion as at 30th June 2019. External debt grew by Kshs.492.67 billion while Domestic debt grew by Kshs.393.1 billion. The increases consisted of disbursements from multilateral organizations and uptake of domestic debt during the reporting period.

In the course of normal reviews during the financial year, OCOB noted that payment of management and commitment fees on loans that were yet to be disbursed long after execution of the loan agreements. Government procedure requires that project planning and approval should precede sourcing for funds, implying that borrowing can only be done when a programme or activity is already scheduled to commence. Therefore, continued payment of obligations on undisbursed loans is not prudent and does not meet any value for money considerations. .

[4.2 Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD) Sector]

The sector plays a key role in the economic and social development of the country by enhancing employment and wealth creation, foreign exchange earnings, the security of land tenure and land management.

text:
[6.1 Introduction]

This chapter highlights issues that affected budget implementation in FY 2019/20. Further, it provides recommendations aimed at improving budget implementation to achieve effective budget execution.
heading_path: 6.1 Introduction

text:
[6.2 Key Issues and Recommendations]

In the course of overseeing budget implementation, the OCOB identified the following key issues which affected budget implementation in the FY 2019/20.
heading_path: 6.2 Key Issues and Recommendations

text:
[6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance]

Budget revision through Supplementary budgets is permissible under Article 223 of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 44 of the Public Finance Management Act, 2012. Budget revision is necessary to rationalize budgetary allocations to non-core activities to release resources for pressing budget needs. Timing of Supplementary Budgets, however should allow time for MDAs to implement the planned activities.

In FY 2019/20, the National Treasury submitted Supplementary Budget I, II and III for approval by Parliament, which mainly rationalized budgetary allocations for non-core activities to release resources for COVID-19 Pandemic interventions and implementation of development activities. The third Supplementary Budget was assented to on 30 th June 2020. As a result, implementing entities did not have adequate time to implement budget activities benefiting from budget revisions. While the budget revision was necessary, some budget performance information such as exchequer issues and incurred expenditure were not considered. As a result, we noted reduction of some budget provisions below the level of expenditures already incurred.

The National Treasury should liaise with MDAs before effecting budget revisions to appropriately align budget allocations to actual performance. Supplementary Budgets should be prepared in good time to allow Parliament to consider and approve them in good time for timely budget implementation.
heading_path: 6.2.1 Timing and Aligning of Supplementary Budget to Actual Performance

text:
[6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget]

Article 228 (6) of the Constitution of Kenya, 2010 and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016 requires the Controller of Budget to submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of budgets of the national and county governments every four months. The Controller of Budget's report is based on quarterly reports on financial and non-financial performance submitted by MDAs in line with Section 83 of the PFM Act, 2012.

During the year, the office noted delays in submission of the quarterly performance reports by some MDAs, causing subsequent delays in reporting and consequently affected the level of oversight of budget implementation by Parliament and other stakeholders.

The Accounting Officers should submit their financial and non-financial performance reports to the OCOB within fifteen days following the end of each quarter in line with Section 83 of the PFM Act, 2012 to facilitate timely reporting on budget implementation.
heading_path: 6.2.2 Delay in Submission of Budget Performance Reports to the Office of the Controller of Budget

text:
[6.2.3 High Level of Pending Bills]

As at 30 th June 2020, MDAs reported pending bills stood at Kshs.53.5 billion. From an analysis of reports received from MDAs, pending bills have been attributed to late submission of invoices and completion certificates by merchants by the end of the financial year, contested Court awards, historical cases and delays in release of exchequer issues, among others.

We recommend all MDAs with pending bills ensure their payments are prioritized as a first charge in the budget implementation cycle for the FY 2020/21 before embarking on other new projects.
heading_path: 6.2.3 High Level of Pending Bills

text:
[6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic]

The first COVID-19 case in Kenya was confirmed in mid-March 2020, prompting the government to institute stringent measures to curb the spread of the disease. While the COVID-19 pandemic is primarily a health crisis with far-reaching economic ramifications, the responses instituted to control its spread have disrupted millions of livelihoods with a disproportionate impact on poor households and the global economic environment.

Given the disruptions occasioned by the actions taken by the government to contain the spread of the COVID-19 pandemic, it is clear that the measures have impacted on all sectors of the economy. In addition, it affected MDAs planned activities resulting in low expenditure of some budget items. These included Travelling, both domestic and foreign, Training and Hospitality.

The OCOB recommends that there is a need for continuous monitoring and reviewing the instituted measures on the impact to the economy by respective institutions to advice promptly on a framework for action aimed at saving lives, protecting households, businesses, and the economy from the possible decline caused by the pandemic.
heading_path: 6.2.4  Economic Effect of the COVID-19 Pandemic

text:
[6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds]

The first COVID-19 case was confirmed in Kenya in mid-March 2020, prompting the Government to introduce stringent measures to curb its spread. The government received funds from donors and other Development Partners which were then set aside through the Ministry of Health funds toward COVID-19 interventions. The purposes of the funds included operationalization of COVID-19 centres, increasing bed capacity at referral hospitals, provision of personal protective equipment to health workers and cash transfer to the Counties, among other interventions.

Some of the programmes funded through Ministry of Health included the Kenya Emergency Response Project (Kshs.5.35 billion), conversion of  a daycare centre to a ward for COVID-19 patients at KNH at Kshs.140 million, operationalization of 300 bed capacity at Kenyatta University Teaching Referral and Research Hospital at Kshs.526.5 million and cash transferred to counties at Kshs.7.71 billion, among others.

The expenditure on COVID-19 pandemic interventions is yet to be audited and the OCOB recommends that the office of the Auditor-General conducts special audits to give an assurance on the value for money and whether the funds were utilized for the intended purpose as required by law.
heading_path: 6.2.5 Special Audit of the utilization of COVID-19 Pandemic Funds

text:
[6.2.6 Evidence of Expenditures above the Exchequer Releases]

Analysis of financial reports submitted to the OCOB by MDAs revealed that some MDAs expenditures were higher than the exchequer releases for the period, especially on development budget. This was partly due to Appropriations-in-Aid, funding from Donors and Development partners which were not released as exchequers through the Consolidated Fund but received directly to MDAs projects and activities as approved in their budget. This appears to be contrary to Article 206 (1) of the Constitution which specifies that, all government revenues should be received in the Consolidated Fund.

The OCOB recommends review of the law which allows MDAs to spend funds before they have been received in the Consolidated Fund as this will enhance transparency and accountability.
heading_path: 6.2.6 Evidence of Expenditures above the Exchequer Releases

text:
[6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases]

In FY 2019/20, the total exchequer issues to National and County Governments was Kshs.2.53 trillion, representing 92.5 per cent of the annual revised net estimates. This was a decrease compared to 95.6 per cent recorded in the FY 2018/19 (Kshs.2.50 trillion in absolute figures). It would be expected that by the end of the financial year, the exchequer releases should be at 100 per cent of the annual estimates.

From the analysis of reports submitted by the MDAs, the low level of expenditure, as well as the pending bills at the end of the year, would be attributable to delays in exchequer releases by the National Treasury. County governments received Kshs.316 billion (91 per cent of the revised net estimates) and this comprised of Kshs.286.8 billion as equitable share and Kshs.29.2 billion as conditional grants. As a result, the equitable share to the counties for June 2020 was not disbursed and was only released in FY 2020/21.

Delay in the release of exchequers delays the implementation of the activities planned by MDAs and Counties and subsequently affects the timely delivery of services. The OCOB recommends that the National Treasury releases funds to the MDAs based on their annual work-plans and cash flow projections. Funds to counties should be released in accordance to Section 17(6) of the PFM Act, 2012 which states that the National Treasury shall at the beginning of every quarter and in any event not later than the fifteenth day from the commencement of the quarter disburse monies to county governments.
heading_path: 6.2.7 Delays in Exchequer Releases

text:
[6.2.8 Level of Public Debt]

As at 30th June 2020, the gross public debt stood at Kshs.6.69 trillion and grew by 15.3 per cent compared to Kshs.5.80 trillion as at 30th June 2019. Disaggregation by External and Internal debt reveals that the former grew by Kshs.492.67 billion while latter grew by Kshs.393.1 billion. Despite the growth in the total loan portfolio, there was a decline in repayment compared to FY 2018/19 when two commercial loans amounting to Kshs.179.3 billion became due.

Actual expenditure of public debt amounted to Kshs.717.65 billion in FY 2019/20, representing 92.1 per cent of the revised gross estimates and 45.6 per cent of the ordinary revenue for the year.

Review of the external debt payments revealed instances where the government continued to pay regular loan commitment and management fees for loans that were yet to be disbursed long after execution of loan agreements. The continued payment of obligations on undisbursed loans is not

prudent and does not meet value for money considerations. The Government is obliged to ensure that its financing needs and payment of obligations are met at the lowest possible cost in the market and uphold the spirit of Article 201(d) of the Constitution which requires prudent and responsible use of public money.

Accordingly, OCOB recommends that, the National Treasury and Planning should undertake an analysis of all loans to identify those that are yet to be disbursed long after execution of the loan agreements. These should be reassessed if still required and appropriate action taken in order to reduce payments on the undisbursed loans
heading_path: 6.2.8 Level of Public Debt
